entries.t: Scythian Word Enters the Western Record
entries.b: Herodotus transcribes the Scythian word kanab- as Greek kánnabis while describing Scythian hemp-steam rituals. This single transliteration is the earliest datable Western record of the cannabis root-word — the ancestor of both 'cannabis' and 'hemp' — linking steppe nomads to the entire European linguistic family.

Fatimid Caliph al-Āmir uses hashīshiyya as a political smear against Syrian Nizari Ismailis — the earliest dated appearance of the hashīsh- word family as a group label. Daftary (1994) shows this meant 'rabble/low-class,' not drug-users. Crusaders adopted the term phonetically, launching the word's journey to European 'assassin.'
entries.src: Daftary, The Assassin Legends (I.B. Tauris, 1994); New World Encyclopedia

entries.t: Ottoman Poets Code Hashish as 'The Secrets'
entries.b: Dervish poet Ḳayġusuz Abdal and Ottoman lyricists adopt esrār ('divine secrets/mysteries') as a literary euphemism for cannabis, encoding Sufi mystical theology into the drug's very name. By mid-16th century this semantic field is firmly established in Ottoman divan poetry — a unique case of a theological concept becoming a drug term.
entries.src: Academia.edu, 'Cannabis (esrār): A Unique Semantic Field in Classical Ottoman Lyric Poetry'

entries.t: De Sacy Cements the Hashish-Assassin Myth
entries.b: French Orientalist Silvestre de Sacy presents his Mémoire linking 'assassin' to Arabic hashshāshīn before the Institut National, drawing on Marco Polo's legendary paradise-garden story (c. 1298). His authoritative framing locks the hashish-murder etymology into Western scholarship for nearly two centuries, until Daftary's 1994 deconstruction.
entries.src: de Sacy, Mémoire (1809); Daftary, The Assassin Legends (1994)

entries.t: The Kaneh-Bosem Dispute: Cannabis in the Bible?
entries.b: Polish anthropologist Sula Benet argues that Hebrew qāneh-bōśem in Exodus 30:23 is cannabis, citing phonetic similarity between Semitic kanabos and Scythian cannabis. Botanist Michael Zohary (Plants of the Bible, 1982) counters that the plant is Acorus calamus. The unresolved debate recurs in every generation of cannabis scholarship.
entries.src: Benet (1936, 1975); Zohary, Plants of the Bible (Cambridge, 1982); Cannabis Culture

facts.fact: Hemp and cannabis are the same word, reached English twice by different routes. Old English hænep (→ hemp) and Greek kánnabis (→ cannabis) both descend from the same Scythian root *kanab-, but hemp traveled through Proto-Germanic with Grimm's Law (k→h, b→p), while cannabis came via Greek and Latin unchanged. English got two words for one plant from one ancient source.

Turkish esrār means 'secrets.' It is the Arabic plural of sirr ('secret') — a core Sufi theological term. Ottoman dervish poets repurposed it as a coded name for cannabis, encoding the mystical-intoxicant equation into the very word. Most modern Turkish speakers have no idea 'secrets' once meant 'weed.'

The 'assassins' may have been named for their poverty, not their drug habits. Farhad Daftary shows that hashīshī was a contemptuous Arabic term for the urban poor — people who could only afford cheap dried scraps (hashīsh = dried herb/fodder). Applied to Nizari Ismailis in 1122 CE as a class insult, it had no proven connection to drug use. Marco Polo's paradise-garden story, written 175 years later, is now considered literary embellishment.

Ganja traveled from Sanskrit to Jamaica in indentured laborers' luggage. South Asian workers brought gāñjā to the Caribbean after 1838; Jamaican Creole adopted it; reggae culture broadcast it globally. One Sanskrit word made a 150-year, 15,000-kilometer journey to become an international slang term.

The Chinese character 麻 (má, hemp/cannabis) is a mini-picture of drying hemp stalks: a roof (广) sheltering two stalks (木 + 木). The same character also means 'numb/tingly' — suggesting ancient Chinese speakers associated the plant directly with its physiological effect in naming it.

Moroccan kīf gave French teenagers a verb. Arabic kayf ('well-being/pleasure') → North African kīf (cannabis) → French slang kiffer ('to really like / to be into'). Classical Arabic philosophy of pleasurable states traveled through a Moroccan drug name into everyday Parisian speech.

Ancient Sanskrit distinguished fiber hemp from drug hemp. Proto-Indo-Iranian *śaṇa- meant industrial fiber hemp (ancestor of Sanskrit śaṇa) while bhanga meant narcotic hemp — a pharmacological distinction encoded in language at least 3,000 years ago, long before modern botany formally recognized Cannabis sativa varieties.
